title: Shloka 123
subtitle: Digits of the moon, the pleasure of poetry, the two attendants

namas.translation: Her substance is the set of measured portions by which the moon is reckoned and the arts are counted.

morphology.note: ātmikā is the feminine of ātmaka, whose -ka suffix already means having, so the word is taken as a derivative of kalātman; the bahuvrīhi reading, she whose self is the digits, is also common.

children.gloss: a sixteenth part, a digit of the moon, an art

namas.translation: She holds sway over the moon's waxing and waning portions and over the arts that share their name.

compound.gloss: the lady who rules the digits

children.gloss: a digit of the moon, an art

namas.translation: Poetry spoken aloud is her recreation, and she is drawn to wherever fine words are being made.

namas.gloss: Served On Left And Right By Ramā And Vāṇī With Chowries
namas.translation: Lakṣmī stands at her left and Sarasvatī at her right, each waving a yak-tail whisk over her.

compound.gloss: attended on either side by Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī bearing chowries

commentary.meaning: The lunar cycle begun in the previous verse narrows here to its unit. A kalā is a digit of the moon, one sixteenth of the whole disc, and the first two names take the two positions the hymn habitually takes together: she is made of the digits, and she is their mistress. The same word also means an art, and it is that second sense that lets the verse turn, without any visible seam, from astronomy to the third name, where poetry recited aloud is called her recreation. The second line then supplies the setting the first line implies. Ramā and Vāṇī — Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī, wealth and speech, the two goddesses to whom most of India actually prays — stand on her left and her right holding yak-tail whisks, which is the posture of court attendants and not of deities. What the verse assembles, name by name, is a durbar: the sovereign, the arts, a recitation in progress, and two fan-bearers. It is also a claim about rank, made without argument and without polemic, simply by describing where everyone is standing.
commentary.history:
Kalā is one of those Sanskrit words whose spread is the whole point. Its basic sense is a small part, and specifically a sixteenth: the moon is reckoned in sixteen digits, of which fifteen wax through the bright fortnight and wane through the dark, while the sixteenth is held never to diminish at all. That unwaning digit, the amā-kalā, is a standing image in Śākta and Śaiva writing for what remains when everything measurable has been subtracted, and it is why the śrīvidyā of sixteen syllables is called Ṣoḍaśī, the sixteenth. From the astronomical sense the word extends to time — the older reckonings divide the day into kāṣṭhās, kalās and muhūrtas — and from measured skill to art in general, which yields the traditional list of sixty-four kalās, the accomplishments of a cultivated person, catalogued by Vātsyāyana among others and running from singing and painting to garland-making and the composition of riddles. In Śaiva and Śākta metaphysics kalā is further a technical term: the fivefold division of the emanated cosmos into kalās in the Siddhānta systems, and in the Kashmirian schools kalā as one of the five sheaths that contract the unlimited agency of consciousness into the limited capacity of an individual. Any of these can be heard in kalātmikā, and the commentators generally decline to choose.

Kalānāthā deserves a note of its own. Kalānātha in the masculine is an ordinary poetic name for the moon, the lord of the digits. The feminine form therefore does two things at once: it says she rules the digits, and it lets her occupy, in the feminine, the position the moon occupies. The pair of names — she is made of them, she rules them — is a structure the sahasranāma uses repeatedly, and it corresponds to a real doctrinal difficulty. If the goddess is the material of the world, she cannot stand outside it to govern it; if she governs it, she is not simply identical with it. The hymn does not resolve this. It states both and moves on, which is closer to the practice of the Upaniṣads than to that of the systematic philosophers.

Kāvyālāpavinodinī rewards being taken apart. Kāvya is what a kavi makes; and kavi, in the Vedic language, does not mean poet but seer, one who perceives what is hidden, so that the classical word for poetry carries an older claim about vision inside it. Ālāpa is speaking, conversation, and in music the unmetred opening in which a rāga is unfolded. Vinodinī comes from vi-√nud, to push away: a vinoda is literally a driving-off, of tedium, and so a diversion or pastime. Put together the name says that poetry spoken aloud is what she does to pass the time — a startlingly light word to use of a supreme deity, and continuous with the older idea that the world itself is her play. The tradition takes the name as a promise as much as a description, which is why poets have addressed her: the goddess Śyāmalā, also called Mātaṅgī, who in this school is Lalitā's minister and the presiding power of speech and music, is the object of a much-loved Daṇḍaka traditionally attributed to Kālidāsa, and the association of poetic gift with the goddess's favour is one of the durable convictions of Sanskrit literary culture.

The long final name is an icon rendered in words. A cāmara is a whisk made from the tail of the yak, and it belongs, with the parasol and the lion-throne, to the standard equipment of kingship; two attendants waving cāmaras on either side is how a South Indian sculptor signals that the central figure is a sovereign. The attendants named here are not minor figures. Ramā, from √ram, to delight, is Lakṣmī, and Vāṇī is speech herself, Sarasvatī. In the Lalitopākhyāna of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, the narrative frame in which this hymn is embedded, the goddess is described in just such a court, and the sahasranāma is elsewhere careful to give her a full administration with ministers and a commander of forces. The compound pairs ramā-vāṇī with savya-dakṣiṇa, left and right, and Sanskrit convention reads two such lists in corresponding order, so that Ramā stands at the left and Vāṇī at the right; this is the reading the standard glosses take, though the placement is a matter on which the iconographic tradition is not perfectly uniform. Doctrinally the arrangement matters more than the sides. Prosperity and eloquence, the two goods most often asked of heaven, are shown here already in service, which is a way of saying that whoever has reached her has passed the point where they need to be requested.
commentary.practice:
The first line is held together by the letter k: kalātmikā, kalānāthā, kāvyālāpavinodinī, five velar stops in eight beats. Let each of them be a clean unaspirated k, made at the back of the mouth with no puff of breath after it — the English k of key has an aspiration that Sanskrit reserves for kh, and using it here turns kalā into something the ear registers as a different word.

In kalātmikā the cluster tm asks the tongue to move from the teeth to the lips with nothing in between: dental t released directly into m, no vowel smuggled in. Kāvyālāpa is a single long stretch of open vowels interrupted by one cluster, vy, and it hides a join — kāvya plus ālāpa, where the final a and the initial ā merge into the long ā you hear. Knowing that keeps you from mislearning the second element as lāpa.

As in the previous verse, the entire second line is one sixteen-syllable name, and it contains the single most treacherous sequence in this stretch of the hymn. Sacāmara ends in ra and ramā begins with ra, so the compound gives -ra-ra- in the middle: sacāmara-ramā. Under speed one of the two disappears and almost nobody notices. Slow the name down at that point deliberately, or count the syllables — sa-cā-ma-ra-ra-mā-vā-ṇī-sa-vya-da-kṣi-ṇa-se-vi-tā, sixteen — until the doubling is secure.

The ṇ of vāṇī and the ṇ of dakṣiṇa are both retroflex, tongue curled back, and the n sounds of vinodinī in the line above are dental. Alternating the two correctly across the verse is a better ear-training exercise than any drill on isolated syllables. The kṣ of dakṣiṇa is the familiar velar plus retroflex sibilant, and sa-vya requires the v and y to be pronounced as a genuine cluster rather than as two syllables.

For archanā the datives are kalātmikāyai, kalānāthāyai, kāvyālāpavinodinyai, and sacāmararamāvāṇīsavyadakṣiṇasevitāyai. The first two are straightforward ā-stems; the third is an ī-stem and contracts to -inyai; the last, like the long name of the preceding verse, has to be taken in one breath, and it is worth breathing deliberately before beginning it rather than discovering halfway through that you cannot finish.

Two things the verse asks of the person chanting it. The first is visual. This is a dhyāna verse in everything but name, and the traditional response to it is to compose the scene: the seated figure, the two women standing at either side, the whisks moving. Recitation in this tradition is not only auditory, and a verse that gives you a tableau expects you to build it.

The second is more pointed. The third name says that the recitation of poetry is her pastime, and the hymn being recited is itself poetry, recited aloud. The person chanting is therefore not describing an activity she enjoys elsewhere; they are performing it. Of all the names in this part of the stotra, kāvyālāpavinodinī is the one that most directly describes what is happening in the room while it is being said.

crossReferences.deva: एवमेवास्य परिद्रष्टुरिमाः षोडश कलाः पुरुषायणाः पुरुषं प्राप्यास्तं गच्छन्ति भिद्येते चासां नामरूपे पुरुष इत्येवं प्रोच्यते स एषोऽकलोऽमृतो भवति ॥
crossReferences.iast: evam evāsya paridraṣṭur imāḥ ṣoḍaśa kalāḥ puruṣāyaṇāḥ puruṣaṃ prāpyāstaṃ gacchanti, bhidyete cāsāṃ nāmarūpe, puruṣa ity evaṃ procyate; sa eṣo 'kalo 'mṛto bhavati ||
crossReferences.translation: Just so, these sixteen parts of the one who beholds all this have the person for their goal; reaching the person they come to rest, their name and form are broken apart, and it is called simply the person. He becomes partless and undying.
crossReferences.relevance: The Upaniṣadic locus for reckoning a whole in sixteen parts, and the passage that gives kalātmikā its resonance. The teaching compares the sixteen kalās to rivers losing their names in the sea, and ends on akala, partless. Set beside it, the two names of this verse are making the complementary claim: she is what the parts are made of and what they answer to, so that being kalātmikā and being their nāthā are not two things.

crossReferences.deva: तव स्तन्यं मन्ये धरणिधरकन्ये हृदयतः पयःपारावारः परिवहति सारस्वतमिव । दयावत्या दत्तं द्रविडशिशुरास्वाद्य तव यत्कवीनां प्रौढानामजनि कमनीयः कवयिता ॥
crossReferences.iast: tava stanyaṃ manye dharaṇidharakanye hṛdayataḥ payaḥpārāvāraḥ parivahati sārasvatam iva | dayāvatyā dattaṃ draviḍaśiśur āsvādya tava yat kavīnāṃ prauḍhānām ajani kamanīyaḥ kavayitā ||
crossReferences.translation: Daughter of the mountain, I think your milk is an ocean of the water of eloquence streaming out of your heart; for the Dravidian child, tasting what you in your compassion gave him, became a poet lovely even among accomplished poets.
crossReferences.relevance: The standard illustration of what kāvyālāpavinodinī implies for the person addressing her — that poetic capacity is something she confers rather than merely enjoys. The verse also joins the two elements this shloka keeps adjacent, since the word for eloquence here is sārasvata, derived from the name of the goddess who stands at her right hand in the fourth name. The Dravidian child of the story is usually identified with the poet Jñānasambandhar, though the identification is later than the poem.

crossReferences.deva: शिवः शक्त्या युक्तो यदि भवति शक्तः प्रभवितुं न चेदेवं देवो न खलु कुशलः स्पन्दितुमपि । अतस्त्वामाराध्यां हरिहरविरिञ्चादिभिरपि प्रणन्तुं स्तोतुं वा कथमकृतपुण्यः प्रभवति ॥
crossReferences.iast: śivaḥ śaktyā yukto yadi bhavati śaktaḥ prabhavituṃ na ced evaṃ devo na khalu kuśalaḥ spanditum api | atas tvām ārādhyāṃ hariharaviriñcādibhir api praṇantuṃ stotuṃ vā katham akṛtapuṇyaḥ prabhavati ||
crossReferences.translation: Only when joined with Śakti is Śiva able to exert power; without her this god is not competent so much as to stir. Since even Hari, Hara and Viriñci must propitiate you, how should one who has laid up no merit manage to bow to you or to praise you?
crossReferences.relevance: The theological premise behind the tableau of the fourth name. If the three great male deities are themselves in the position of worshippers, then two goddesses holding whisks at her side is a consistent picture rather than a rhetorical exaggeration. Reading the two passages together also shows the difference in method: the Saundaryalaharī argues the point, while the sahasranāma simply describes the room and lets the arrangement carry the argument.

references.title: The Practical Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: Vaman Shivram Apte (rev. ed., Prasad Prakashan, Poona, 1957–59)
references.note: Better than Monier-Williams for literary vocabulary, and the right place to read the entry on kalā, which runs to a column and a half and gives the citations from poetry that show how a single word does duty for a lunar digit, a unit of time, a fine art and a metaphysical part. The sixty-four arts are listed there too, which saves hunting for them.

references.title: The Saundaryalaharī, or Flood of Beauty
references.author: ed. and tr. W. Norman Brown (Harvard Oriental Series 43, 1958)
references.note: The scholarly edition, with the Sanskrit, a literal translation, and an introduction that is candid about the poem's attribution to Śaṅkara being untenable. Brown's notes on verse 75 and on the milk-of-poetry motif are the quickest way to see how the poetic and the ritual readings of the same verse diverge.

references.title: The Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa
references.author: tr. G. V. Tagare (Ancient Indian Tradition and Mythology, Motilal Banarsidass)
references.note: The Lalitopākhyāna, which occupies the later part of the third section, is the narrative frame in which this hymn is transmitted, and it is where the goddess's court — her ministers, her commander, her attendants — is described at length. The translation is serviceable rather than elegant, but it is the only complete English version, and reading the surrounding story changes how the courtly names in this verse sound.

references.title: Kamasutra
references.author: Vātsyāyana; tr. Wendy Doniger and Sudhir Kakar (Oxford World's Classics, 2002)
references.note: Cited here only for the catalogue of the sixty-four arts in the first book, which is the standard list behind the sense of kalā as accomplishment. It is worth reading precisely because it is so unmystical: singing, painting, cooking, arranging beds, teaching parrots to talk. That this is the same word the hymn uses for the digits of the moon is a fact about Sanskrit that no translation can preserve.

references.title: Sri Lalitha Sahasranamam
references.author: M. S. Subbulakshmi (His Master's Voice / Saregama)
references.note: The recording by which most people in India know the text, and still the most useful for learning it. Her tempo is deliberate enough that the long sixteen-syllable names of this verse and the one before it can be followed syllable by syllable, and the doubled ra-ra in sacāmararamā is audible rather than swallowed, which is exactly the point at which unaided reciters go wrong.
